strengths: Clear and well-motivated research question: deriving principled, rather than heuristic, parameterisations for scaling predictive coding networks (PCNs), building on the influential µP/mean-field literature for BP.

The core theoretical contributions are well-scoped and clearly characterised: Theorem 1 (width-stable feature-learning parameterisations for linear PCNs coincide with BP's set, Eq. 15) and Theorem 2 (depth exponent α = 1/2 for residual networks) are proven via careful derivations in Appendices A.4–A.5, following the rigorous style of Bordelon & Pehlevan (2022b).

The convergence results (Corollaries 3.2 and 4.2) provide a non-trivial strengthening of prior work: the paper clearly delineates its delta over Ishikawa et al. (2024) (necessity vs. mere existence) and Innocenti et al. (2025) (convergence throughout training vs. only at initialisation), and the related-work discussion (§A.2) is unusually thorough and fair.

Empirical verification is broad and well-matched to the theory: linear and nonlinear models (residual MLPs, CNNs trained on ImageNet-1k, nano-GPT-style transformers), multiple datasets, optimisers and losses, with quantitative checks (cosine similarities between PC and BP gradients, verification of the s(θ) = 1 + Θ(L/N) scaling in Figure 3).

The empirical observation that the PC-specific 'fast saddle-to-saddle' regime is unstable in both width and depth (Takeaway 2) is a genuinely useful negative result that constrains where PC can offer advantages over BP.

Honest and substantive limitations section: linearity of the theory, incomplete inference convergence, non-locality of attention, short training runs (100 steps), and untested hyperparameter transfer are all acknowledged rather than obscured.
Good reproducibility: code is released as part of a JAX library, experimental details and compute resources are documented (§A.8, §A.9), and results are averaged over seeds where reported.
weaknesses: The theoretical results are restricted to linear networks with exactly equilibrated activities; the extension to nonlinear architectures rests on heuristic parameterisation extensions (§A.6) and empirical support rather than proof, so the headline claim 'PC converges to BP' is only established for linear models.

The regime in which convergence is guaranteed (N ≫ L) is precisely the regime where PC has no demonstrated practical advantage over BP, and the regime where PC has shown advantages (fast saddle-to-saddle dynamics) is shown to be unstable; thus the practical payoff is currently mostly a promise contingent on accelerating PC inference (e.g., analog hardware speculation).

Experiments are short (100 training steps) and do not demonstrate that PC trains competitive models to convergence under these parameterisations, nor is the µP hyperparameter-transfer property validated, limiting the demonstrated practical impact.

Some empirical fragility remains: layer normalisation breaks PC-to-BP convergence in the transformer experiments, and MLPs diverge from BP at large depth regardless of width (Figures A.7–A.8), indicating the theory's reach in practice is narrower than the headline suggests.

Incremental novelty relative to closest related work: the paper itself concedes the result recovers Ishikawa et al. (2024)'s parameterisation and Innocenti et al. (2025)'s depth scaling, with the contribution being necessity of these parameterisations and rigorous justification; readers outside the PC/local-learning niche may find the contribution specialised.

The biological claims ('BP can be implemented by the brain') are speculative given the model's abstractions (scalar outputs, no biases, equilibrated inference assumptions) and are more motivational than supported.

strengths: The paper delivers a clean and well-executed theoretical contribution: it proves that the set of width- and depth-stable feature-learning parameterisations for linear predictive coding networks is exactly the same as for backpropagation (Theorems 1-2), and that PC gradients converge to BP gradients when N >> L (Corollaries 3.2 and 4.2). The derivations in Appendices A.4-A.5 are careful, self-contained, and follow established techniques (Bordelon & Pehlevan 2022b; Yang et al. 2023) in a way that specialists can verify.

The necessity claim ('if one wants muP desiderata, then muP is the only option') strengthens prior existence results, notably Ishikawa et al. (2024), and provides a principled justification for the heuristic parameterisation used by Innocenti et al. (2025) to train 100+ layer PCNs. This is a genuine advance in the understanding of PC scalability.

The empirical program is well aligned with the theory: the L/N scaling of the equilibrated energy rescaling (Figure 3, Eq. 19) is directly verified against theory, and convergence of PC to BP gradients is demonstrated on linear and nonlinear residual MLPs, CNNs (ImageNet-1k), and nano-GPT-style transformers, across optimisers and loss functions (Figures 1, 2, 4, and the extensive appendix).

The limitations discussion is unusually honest and substantive: it clearly states that the theory is linear-only, that convergence requires exact activity equilibration, that the fast saddle-to-saddle regime unique to PC is unstable in width and depth, and that experiments were only run for 100 steps due to inference cost. The authors also correctly note (Figure A.5) that their results do not rule out other notions of stable parameterisation.
The comparison to related work (A.2) is thorough and fair, precisely delineating what is new relative to Ishikawa et al. (2024) and Innocenti et al. (2025).
weaknesses: The central theoretical results are confined to linear networks with exactly equilibrated activities, which is a strong restriction. The extension to nonlinear models is purely empirical and heuristic (parameterisations for CNNs/transformers are adapted 'heuristically', A.6), so the 'hard constraints on scalable parameterisations for PC' claimed in the abstract and Section 6.2 are over-stated: they are hard constraints only within the considered linear 'abcd' family and under the muP desiderata. The paper acknowledges this, but the framing sometimes exceeds the evidence.

Incremental novelty relative to prior work. The equilibrated energy (Eq. 5) and the PC-vs-BP correspondence at large width were already established (Ishikawa et al. 2024; Innocenti et al. 2024a, 2025). The new contribution is the necessity argument, the depth extension, and the throughout-training (vs initialisation-only) convergence result. This is useful but modest in scope, and the paper's positioning ('goes significantly beyond' Ishikawa et al.) somewhat inflates the delta.

The N >> L regime limits practical significance. While the authors argue modern LLMs are wider than deep, depth is not negligible relative to width, and the theory gives no guarantee (and experiments show divergence, e.g. Figures A.7-A.8, A.13-A.14) in the regimes of most practical interest for deep models. Combined with the prohibitive inference cost (up to 100k activity steps for convergence), the practical payoff of the result remains speculative.

Experimental depth is thin: all models were trained for only 100 steps (A.8), no model was trained to convergence, and the predicted muP hyperparameter transfer property was not validated. As a result, the claim that 'our linear theory remains valid for nonlinear models' rests on short-horizon gradient cosine similarities rather than end-to-end training behaviour.

Some experimental details undermine confidence in the nonlinear claims: layer normalisation had to be removed from the transformer 'because it breaks convergence of PC to BP' (A.8), and the ImageNet CNN used very narrow widths (2-32 output channels). These choices constrain how representative the results are of realistic settings.

Reproducibility is imperfect: the code URL is blank in the manuscript (pages 8 and 29 state 'Code to reproduce all the results is available at' with no link), though the stated JAX library dependency and detailed hyperparameters in A.8-A.9 partially mitigate this. There are also typographical issues (e.g. 'as long an an activity equilibrium', 'derive the with scaling exponents', 'does not not converge') that suggest insufficient proofreading.

strengths: Well-posed research question with a clear, cleanly stated set of theoretical results: the set of width- and depth-stable feature-learning parameterisations for PC is exactly the same as for BP (Theorems 1-2), and PC gradients converge to BP gradients when N >> L (Corollaries 3.2 & 4.2).

The results go meaningfully beyond closest prior work: Ishikawa et al. (2024) only showed existence of a BP-implementing parameterisation, while this paper proves necessity (uniqueness) under the µP/mean-field desiderata; Innocenti et al. (2025) proved energy-to-loss convergence only at initialisation, while this paper proves it throughout training.

The derivations in the appendix (§A.4-A.5) are systematic and carefully check each desideratum, including the PC-specific rescaling term s(θ), with the theoretical scaling s(θ) - 1 = Θ(L/N) empirically verified (Figure 3, A.9-A.10).

Strong empirical support across model classes: linear and nonlinear residual MLPs, CNNs trained on ImageNet-1k, and nano-GPT-style transformers, with gradient cosine similarity between PC and BP increasing with width as predicted; multiple datasets, optimisers, and loss functions.

Exceptionally honest and thorough limitations discussion (§6.3): linearity of the theory, unvalidated hyperparameter transfer, PC inference cost, non-local attention, and the fact that experiments only ran 100 steps. The paper does not oversell its claims (e.g., it explicitly notes it cannot rule out other stable parameterisations where PC does not converge to BP).
Good reproducibility: code released as part of a JAX library, detailed experimental settings (§A.8), compute resources reported (§A.9).
weaknesses: Theoretical novelty is somewhat incremental: the core machinery (equilibrated energy, rescaling s(θ)) comes from prior work (Innocenti et al., 2024a; Ishikawa et al., 2024), and the analysis is largely a careful transfer of known BP scaling calculations (Bordelon & Pehlevan, 2022b; Yang et al., 2023) to the PC energy. The authors themselves admit 'physics-level rigour' rather than full mathematical rigour.

The central theoretical results are confined to linear networks with exactly equilibrated activities; the nonlinear case (arguably the practically relevant one) is supported only empirically, and nonlinear experiments require very large inference budgets (up to 100k steps), so 'equilibrium reached' is a strong practical assumption.

Empirical evaluation is limited in ways that temper the practical significance: all experiments run only 100 training steps and measure gradient cosine similarity rather than task performance at convergence; hyperparameter transfer (the main practical payoff of µP) is predicted but not validated; the ImageNet CNNs are very narrow (2-32 channels) and the transformer required removing layer normalisation, deviating from standard practice.

The headline finding has a partly negative character: in the only regime where PC is stable and feature-learning at scale, it reduces to BP, which undermines the distinctive advantages previously claimed for PC (e.g., the fast saddle-to-saddle regime is shown to be unstable). This is a valuable clarification but limits how much new capability the work enables.

The 'wider than deep' convergence condition (N >> L) excludes exactly the deep, parameter-efficient regimes of modern interest for local learning; the practical path to exploiting the layer-parallelism of PC at L-layer speed-up remains speculative and deferred to future analog-hardware work.

Some derivation steps rely on heuristics, e.g., dropping higher-order terms in the recursion of Eq. 120-121, and averaging/typical-case arguments for weight norms; these are standard in the scaling literature but mean the theorems are less airtight than their statement suggests.

strengths: The central theoretical contribution is clean and rigorous: the paper proves (for linear MLPs and linear residual networks) that the set of width-/depth-stable and feature-learning parameterisations for PC is exactly the same as for BP (Theorems 1-2), and quantifies the convergence of PC gradients to BP gradients with explicit rates (O(N^-1) for MLPs at fixed depth, O(L/N) for residual networks in joint limits with L/N -> 0). Full derivations are provided in a detailed appendix.

The results go meaningfully beyond prior work: relative to Ishikawa et al. (2024), the paper proves necessity (muP is the only scalable parameterisation under the stated desiderata) rather than mere existence, extends the analysis to depth, and generalises the initialisation-only convergence result of Innocenti et al. (2025) to hold throughout training. The analysis of the 'fast saddle-to-saddle' PC regime as unstable with both width and depth is a genuinely useful insight that constrains where PC advantages over BP can exist.

Comprehensive empirical validation that matches the scope of the theory: linear networks (toy tasks, CIFAR-10, Fashion-MNIST), nonlinear residual MLPs, CNNs trained on ImageNet-1k with cross-entropy, and nano-GPT-style transformers, with multiple optimisers (GD, SGD, Adam), loss functions, seeds, and verification of the predicted s(theta) = 1 + Theta(L/N) scaling against theory (Figures 3, A.9, A.10). Compute resources are documented and code is released.

Honest and thorough limitations section (linearity of the theory, reliance on exact inference equilibrium, inference cost, unvalidated hyperparameter transfer, non-local attention), plus a careful related-work discussion (A.2) that fairly delineates contributions from Ishikawa et al., Innocenti et al., and Goemaere et al.

The implications are clearly articulated: the results give hard constraints on scalable PC parameterisations (guiding practice, e.g. validating the muPC choice of alpha = 1/2) and suggest a concrete route by which wide-than-deep networks could implement BP with purely local updates.
weaknesses: The theory is restricted to linear networks and exact inference equilibrium; all nonlinear claims rest on empirical cosine-similarity evidence and heuristic extensions of the parameterisation to CNNs/transformers. The paper is upfront about this, but it limits the theoretical reach of the contribution.

The headline result is partly a 'negative' result: under any stable, feature-learning parameterisation, PC converges to BP at large width, so PC offers no algorithmic benefit in exactly the regime where it is scalable. The practical payoff (parallelisable weight updates, biological plausibility) depends on substantially accelerating PC inference, which is not demonstrated here.

The experiments are short (100 training steps); no model is trained to convergence, no PC-vs-BP performance comparison is provided, and the predicted hyperparameter transfer property of muP is not validated. This leaves open whether the theory is useful for actual training at scale, as the authors themselves acknowledge.

Some experimental setup choices are restrictive or under-justified: layer normalisation had to be removed from the transformer to observe PC-BP convergence, PC inference required up to 100k steps for the deepest models, and high gradient alignment for deeper nonlinear networks only held after many inference steps, which strains the 'equilibrium reached' assumption in practice.

Practitioners using the standard parameterisation are told PC (like BP) is unstable at large width, but the paper provides little guidance beyond the derived scalings; the depth analysis assumes L/N -> 0 and residual architectures, and the MLP results break down at large depth (Figures A.7-A.8), so the applicability envelope is narrower than the abstract might suggest.

strengths: The theoretical analysis is careful and transparent: the 'abcd' parameterisation framework is well-motivated, the derivations for linear MLPs and linear residual networks are laid out step by step in the appendix, and the paper is honest that the analysis carries only 'physics-level rigour' rather than full measure-theoretic rigor.

The necessity result (Theorems 1-2: the set of stable and feature-learning parameterisations for linear PCNs is identical to BP's) is a genuine strengthening over Ishikawa et al. (2024), which only showed existence, and it resolves an open question left by Innocenti et al. (2025) regarding the depth feature-learning desideratum.

The empirical program is broad for a theory paper: gradient alignment is validated on linear and nonlinear residual networks, CNNs (with ImageNet-1k), and nano-GPT-style transformers, across different optimisers, loss functions, and datasets, with multiple seeds where reported.

The paper contextualises its negative-sounding result (PC converges to BP at large width) constructively, e.g., that BP could in principle be implemented by a local, layer-parallel algorithm in wider-than-deep regimes, and it discusses the unstable fast saddle-to-saddle PC regime of prior work.

Limitations (linearity of the theory, inference cost, short training runs, non-locality of attention) are discussed candidly in §6.3, and code is stated to be released within an existing JAX PCN library.
weaknesses: The central theory applies only to linear networks. The nonlinear experiments are purely empirical and cannot confirm that the stability/feature-learning characterisation carries over; the paper itself acknowledges DMFT extension as future work. This leaves the headline claim ('constrains the parameterisations that are scalable with PC') only partially supported for architectures people actually care about.

The practical significance is questionable, and largely speculative. The main empirical finding is that PC ≈ BP at large width, which by itself offers no advantage over BP; the suggested payoff (O(1) sequential weight-update cost, brain-like implementation) is contingent on accelerating PC inference, which the paper only speculates about (analog hardware). Notably, the widely-cited unique PC benefit (fast saddle-to-saddle dynamics) is shown to be unstable, so the paper's contribution to the 'why PC?' question is mostly negative.

The convergence regime (L/N → 0) is narrow, and the empirical alignment is only 'almost perfect' asymptotically: at practically relevant widths the cosine similarities in Figures 1, 4, and A.13-A.14 show substantial deviation, and alignment breaks down entirely for deeper MLPs (Figures A.7-A.8), limiting the reach of the result.

Experiments are shallow in an important sense: all models are trained for only 100 steps, the transformer required removing layer normalisation (a core component of modern architectures) to obtain alignment, and residual MLP inference needed up to 100k GD iterations per step. Hyperparameter transfer — the main practical selling point of µP-style parameterisations — is not validated at all, only 'predicted' to hold.

Novelty is incremental relative to the closest prior work: the width result substantially overlaps with Ishikawa et al. (2024) and the residual-network result builds directly on Innocenti et al. (2025) and Bordelon et al. (2023); the main new ingredients are the uniqueness/necessity claims and the O(L/N) error bound, which are modest technical advances.

There are signs of fragility in the empirical-theory bridge: the discrepancy with Innocenti et al. (2025) (their empirical correspondence deteriorating with training) is attributed to their numerical issues rather than examined directly, and several key design choices (Adam with η0=1e-3, removal of weight decay 'for visualisation purposes') are heuristic rather than derived, even though the paper's contribution is precisely to derive principled parameterisations.

The writing, while generally clear, relies heavily on the appendix: multiple main-text takeaways (learning regimes, MLP depth fragility) are only fully substantiated in supplementary figures, and the heavy back-referencing makes the main results harder to assess self-contained.

strengths: The main theoretical contribution is stronger than prior work in the area: rather than just showing existence of a µP-like parameterisation for linear PCNs (Ishikawa et al., 2024), Theorems 1-2 prove that within the general 'abcd' parameterisation family, the µP/mean-field scalings are the *only* ones satisfying stability and feature-learning desiderata for PC — a genuinely non-trivial uniqueness result that constrains the space of scalable PC parameterisations.

The joint width-depth analysis for linear residual networks (Theorem 2, Corollary 4.2 with O(L/N) error) is a clear generalisation of Innocenti et al. (2025), which proved convergence of the objectives only at initialisation; here convergence of gradients holds throughout training in the L/N → 0 regime.

The empirical validation is unusually thorough for a theory paper: linear and nonlinear networks, MLPs, CNNs on ImageNet-1k, nano-GPT-style transformers on Tiny Shakespeare, multiple optimisers (GD, Adam), loss functions (MSE, cross-entropy), and activations, with many supporting appendix figures (A.1-A.24) verifying each prediction, including negative cases where theory does not apply (e.g., MLP gradient divergence at depth in Figures A.7-A.14).

The paper provides valuable insight by showing that the fast saddle-to-saddle regime where PC benefits over BP (Innocenti et al., 2024a) is intrinsically unstable with width and depth (Takeaway 2), unifying and clarifying the PC literature.

Limitations are discussed honestly and extensively (linear-only theory, equilibrium assumption, 100-step training, inference cost), and the code, experimental details, and compute resources are well documented, supporting reproducibility.
Derivations in the appendix are careful and self-contained, with explicit tracking of width and depth exponents, and important assumptions (e.g., L/N = O(1) vs L/N → 0) stated precisely.
weaknesses: The theoretical results are restricted to linear networks; all claims about nonlinear architectures rest on heuristic extensions and empirical cosine-similarity observations rather than theory. The central novelty of the analysis (that PC inherits BP's stable parameterisations via the equilibrated energy rescaling s(θ) = 1 + Θ(L/N)) follows fairly directly from the known form of the equilibrated energy, so the mathematical machinery largely mirrors prior BP analyses (Bordelon & Pehlevan, 2022b; Yang et al., 2023; Bordelon et al., 2023).

The practical significance of the headline result is tempered by the equilibrium assumption: achieving gradient alignment at large width required up to 100k inference steps (§A.9), so the suggestion that PC could 'implement BP at scale' with local updates remains far from demonstrated; no experiment trains a model to convergence, and the predicted hyperparameter transfer of µP is not validated.

Several empirical settings use very small models relative to the scaling claims (e.g., CNNs with Cout as low as 2 on ImageNet, transformer width starting at N=8, 100 training steps), so the asymptotic regime is only loosely probed for the nonlinear cases.

Some framings risk overstating scope: 'necessarily µP is the only scalable parameterisation for PC' holds only within the considered parameterisation family and desiderata set (acknowledged in Figure A.5 and §6.3, but the headline statements in §6.2 are less qualified).
The experiments in §5 rely on a representative run for Figure 4 cosine similarities; while results are stated to be consistent across seeds, error bars are not reported there.
